First Frost Squash Stew

The first frost came early this year, and with it the urge to stand over a pot of something slow. This stew began as a way to use up the last of the garden: a few knobbly carrots, a fistful of sage, and a squash that had grown larger than anyone expected. It has since become the thing we make on the first properly cold evening, every year, without discussion.

Start by softening the onions in a wide pot with plenty of oil and a good pinch of salt, and be patient about it. They should go soft and sweet and just begin to colour, which takes a full fifteen minutes over a low flame. Add the carrots, the squash cut into rough chunks, and the sage, then stir everything around until the vegetables are glossy and fragrant.

Pour in enough stock to cover, bring the pot to a gentle simmer, and leave it alone for forty minutes with the lid tilted. The squash will collapse into the broth and thicken it without any help. Taste near the end and adjust the salt, then finish with a squeeze of lemon and a spoonful of yoghurt on each bowl. It keeps for four days in the refrigerator and is better on the second.

If you like it thicker, mash a few of the squash chunks against the side of the pot with the back of a spoon. If you like it brothier, add another cup of stock. Either way, serve it with something crusty for the bowl, and make sure there is butter on the table, because there should always be butter on the table when it is this cold outside.
